Q204.L1t: A stoma is a surgically created opening that brings bowel or urinary tract onto the abdominal wall so waste can leave the body.
Q204.L2t: Stomas such as colostomies, ileostomies and urostomies may be temporary or permanent depending on the underlying condition and the surgery performed.
Q204.L3t: Bowel resection for a malignant tumour often leaves no safe route for normal faecal passage, and cancer is among the leading indications for surgery that results in a stoma.
Q204.L4t: Cancer of the bowel or bladder is one of the most common reasons for a stoma to be formed.
Q204.L2f: Stomas are always permanent, and a temporary stoma is never used to let a surgical join in the bowel heal.
Q204.L3f: Irritable bowel syndrome causes structural damage to the bowel that commonly needs surgical resection, so it is a leading reason for stomas.
Q204.L4f: Irritable bowel syndrome is one of the most common reasons for a stoma to be formed.

Q205.L1t: Inhaled drugs act directly on the airways and need correct technique, because poor technique greatly reduces how much medicine reaches the lungs.
Q205.L2t: Much of the dose from a metered-dose inhaler can land in the mouth and throat, where it does not help the lungs.
Q205.L3t: Particles settle in the small airways by sedimentation when airflow stops, so a pause at the end of a slow, deep breath in lets the drug deposit there.
Q205.L4t: The patient should hold their breath after breathing in on using the inhaler, so the drug has time to settle in the lower airways.
Q205.L2f: Spacer devices raise the amount of drug that hits the throat, so they are not used for patients with poor coordination.
Q205.L3f: Rapid shallow breaths drive the drug particles deeper into the lungs, because fast repeated inhalations carry more aerosol past the upper airway.
Q205.L4f: Taking lots of small, quick breaths in is the way to get most of the drug into the lower airways.

Q206.L1t: Mitochondria are double-membrane organelles that produce most of a cell's ATP through aerobic respiration.
Q206.L2t: The mitochondrion has an outer membrane, an inner membrane folded into cristae, an intermembrane space and an inner matrix.
Q206.L3t: The proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis must be built across the inner membrane, so the carriers that pump protons are fixed within that membrane.
Q206.L4t: The inner mitochondrial membrane contains the protein complexes of the electron transport chain.
Q206.L2f: Mitochondria have a single membrane with no folds, and they are found only in cells that lack a nucleus.
Q206.L3f: Mitochondria are the main cellular site for storing energy reserves, so their inner membrane is packed with stored carbohydrate polymers.
Q206.L4f: Glycogen molecules are what is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
